note: Element pages of the Chip Explorer (/explorer/element/). Element data (data/<id>.json + .cells.bin) is written by tools/explorer_elem_export.py pack into the fleet-viz deploy dir, not committed. Story captions are templates: {a.key} reads the metrics the page computes from element a's exported data (see elem.js metrics()), so every number on screen comes from the routed DB or its closure record.

pages.title: BF element: hierarchical column vs flat half-rate
pages.summary: Two routed versions of the BF weight-multiply element side by side: the flat half-rate block that closed first and one column of the hierarchical full-rate design the owner adopted, both drawn from their final routed databases.

story.title: Two routed BF blocks, side by side
story.cap: {pos.A}: the flat half-rate BF block, {a.n} placed cells around {a.macros} ROM macros in {a.W|1} × {a.H|1} µm. {pos.B}: one column of the hierarchical full-rate BF, {b.n} cells around {b.macros} ROM macros in {b.W|1} × {b.H|1} µm. A full hierarchical pair is a front block plus two such columns.
story.why: Both pictures are the final routed databases the sign-off verdicts were computed from ({pos.a} TT {a.recTT} / FF {a.recFF} ps, {pos.b} TT {b.recTT} / FF {b.recFF} ps), not drawings.

story.title: Colour is the RTL block each cell implements
story.cap: Every dot is a placed standard cell, coloured by the part of the RTL it belongs to. The purple rectangles are the ROM macros that hold the weights; the logic is packed around them.
story.why: The placer keeps each block's cells together, which keeps the wires inside a block short.

story.title: One clock pin feeds every flop
story.cap: The clock enters at one pin (diamond). In the {pos.a} block a tree of {a.clkNodes} buffers, {a.clkDepth} levels deep, carries it to {a.leaves} flops; the column needs {b.clkNodes} buffers, {b.clkDepth} levels deep, for {b.leaves} flops.
story.why: Each level adds delay, so a bigger block gets its clock later.

story.title: When the clock edge arrives
story.cap: Each flop is now coloured by when the clock edge reaches it at the typical corner (dark = early, yellow = late, one scale for both). The median flop in the {pos.a} block gets it after {a.tt.p50} ps, which is longer than the whole 833 ps cycle at 1.2 GHz; in the column the median is {b.tt.p50} ps.
story.why: Flops that trade data with neighbouring blocks see this delay. The hierarchical pair closes its block-to-block timing only because the die clock delays the front block by 367 ps (TT) to match the columns (record results/rtl/s81_bf_arch_20261009/compose/summary.json).

story.title: Inside a block, the spread is what counts
story.cap: Within the flat block almost every flop gets the edge inside a {a.tt.p9901} ps window (1st to 99th percentile). The column's window is wider, {b.tt.p9901} ps: its BF16 lane tiles get the clock at about {b.clkByTop.g_bf.p50} ps, while its FP8 lane pipelines, accumulation chains and reduction tree get it earlier, at about {b.clkByTop.g_tr5.p50} ps.
story.why: On any path, what matters for hold is the difference between the launching and capturing flop's arrival. The column's two waves follow its structure (the BF16 tiles are clocked through their own tile clock gates), but a path that crosses between the waves has to absorb the difference.

story.title: At the fast corner, where hold is checked
story.cap: At the FF corner the window is {a.ff.p9901} ps in the {pos.a} block and {b.ff.p9901} ps in the column. The worst hold path in the {pos.a} block launches at {a.hold0.launch} ps and captures at {a.hold0.capture} ps; in the column it launches at {b.hold0.launch} ps and captures at {b.hold0.capture} ps, {b.hold0.skew} ps later.
story.why: A capture clock that arrives later than the launch clock lets fast data overwrite the value before it is held, so those paths need added delay.

story.title: The price: hold-fix buffers
story.cap: Yellow cells are the delay buffers the hold repair inserted: {a.holdBuf} in the {pos.a} block ({a.holdPct|1} % of its cells) and {b.holdBuf} in the column ({b.holdPct|1} %). Per cell, the column pays more hold repair than the flat block.
story.why: Hold buffers are pure delay: they cost area and power and take routing tracks. This is the cost side of the hierarchical choice, shown honestly.

story.title: Worst setup path, cycle by cycle
story.cap: The red line is the slowest register-to-register path at the typical corner, drawn through its placed pins. It closes with {a.setupWNS} ps to spare in the {pos.a} block and {b.setupWNS} ps in the column.
story.why: The flat block reaches its margin with half-rate (multicycle) constraints on its datapath (half_mc.sdc in its sign-off SDC list); the column closes every path in a single 833 ps cycle.

story.title: Why the owner chose the hierarchical BF
story.cap: The choice is a rate decision. Run at full rate, the hierarchical BF prices the DeepSeek ROM design at 1,553.4 tok/s per user (AR) against 1,447.7 for the half-rate flat block, +7.3 % (record results/rtl/s81_bf_arch_20261009/compose/price.json, main a5a6af2c5). The physical cost is visible here: more hold repair per column and a clock plan that offsets the front block.
story.why: The column shown is col600, the closed hierarchical evidence. The adopted compact column (450 × 220 µm) was still routing when this page was built and replaces it here when it closes.
